When sunlight hits a raindrop, the light bends as it enters, a process called refraction, and different colors bend by slightly different amounts, which is why they spread apart into a band. Some of that light also bounces off the inside back of the droplet before exiting, a step known as internal reflection, sending it back out at a slightly different angle for each color. Because millions of droplets are doing this at once, we see the whole arc rather than a single point, and that's really all a rainbow amounts to, sunlight sorted into its component colors by water acting like tiny prisms.

The Kerr-Newman solution generalizes the Schwarzschild metric to account for both angular momentum and charge, yielding an outer event horizon at r+ = M + sqrt(M² - a² - Q²) in geometrized units. Rotation introduces frame dragging, quantified by the metric's off-diagonal g_tφ term, and produces an ergosphere outside the horizon where no observer can remain static relative to infinity. Within this region, the Penrose process permits extraction of rotational energy by splitting an infalling particle such that one fragment carries negative energy across the horizon, reducing the hole's angular momentum while the other escapes with more energy than the original particle possessed. Superradiant scattering of bosonic fields achieves an analogous amplification without particle infall, relevant to constraints on ultralight axion-like particles via black hole spin-down measurements. At the quantum level, Hawking radiation arises from vacuum-mode mixing across the horizon, with a Hawking temperature inversely proportional to mass; for a solar-mass hole this yields a temperature many orders of magnitude below the cosmic microwave background, meaning net absorption dominates until the universe cools further. The information paradox concerns whether the resulting thermal-looking radiation is truly information-free, in apparent tension with unitary evolution, a tension partially addressed by recent replica wormhole calculations of the entanglement entropy via the Page curve.

Compiler pipeline notes, study guide

- Lexer: tokenizes raw source text into a stream of tokens (identifiers, literals, keywords, punctuation), stripping whitespace and comments along the way.
- Parser: consumes the token stream and builds an abstract syntax tree according to the language's grammar, typically using recursive descent or an LR-style table-driven approach.
- Semantic analysis: walks the AST to check types, resolve identifiers against scope, and catch errors like undeclared variables or mismatched argument counts.
- IR generation: lowers the AST into an intermediate representation, often something like three-address code or SSA form, which is easier to analyze and transform than the original syntax tree.
- Optimization passes: run over the IR doing things like constant folding, dead code elimination, common subexpression elimination, and loop-invariant code motion, usually iterated until a fixed point or a pass budget is hit.
- Register allocation: maps the IR's virtual registers onto the target machine's limited physical registers, spilling to memory when there aren't enough to go around; graph coloring is the classic approach here.
- Code generation: emits actual machine instructions for the target architecture, handling instruction selection and scheduling.
- Linking: combines object files and resolves external symbol references into a final executable.

Let me explain this the way I'd explain it to my own grandchildren, taking my time over every part of it, because I think it deserves a careful, gentle explanation rather than a rushed one. Imagine your body has its very own little army inside it, an army whose only job is to protect you from tiny troublemakers called germs, the kind of germs that make you cough or get a fever. Most of the time this army doesn't know what a brand new troublemaker looks like, so if a nasty germ shows up for the first time, the army takes a while to figure out how to fight it, and that's often when you feel really sick. A vaccine is like showing your army a wanted poster of the troublemaker ahead of time, except the poster is actually a tiny, harmless piece or a weakened copy of the germ, not the real dangerous thing at all, so it can't make you sick the way the real germ would. Once your army studies that poster, it learns exactly what the troublemaker looks like and practices building the perfect tools to catch it, tools we can just think of as little sticky nets. Then if the real germ ever sneaks in later, your army already recognizes it right away, pulls out the nets it already built, and fights it off fast, often before you even notice you were sick at all. That's really the whole trick behind a vaccine: a safe practice round so your body's army is ready long before the real fight ever happens, and I think that's rather a wonderful thing when you stop to think about it.

ok tryin to explain this to my roommate since he kept asking after that last shake. so basically most quakes happen along faults, those are just cracks in the earths crust where two big rock slabs are pushed against each other. they dont slide smoothly, they kinda stick due to friction and stress just builds up over years, sometimes decades, like bending a stick further n further. eventually the stress gets bigger than the friction holding it n the rocks suddenly slip, releasing all that stored energy at once as seismic waves, those are just vibrations that travel through the ground n shake everything on top.

theres two main kinds that matter for what you feel, p waves get there first, theyre faster but usually less violent, then s waves show up a bit after and do most of the actual shaking damage. scientists use the gap between when each wave arrives at different stations to figure out roughly where the whole thing started underground.

also ppl mix up magnitude n intensity a lot, magnitude is just one number for the whole event based on how much energy got released, but intensity is about how strong the shaking actually felt in a specific spot, so the same quake can feel way different in two towns depending how close n what kind of ground theyre on, soft soil shakes way more than solid rock.
